one_line: Dissects Lithos Metal's "200 tok/s" Qwen 27B claim on Apple M5 Max: a projection, with ~80 tok/s measured end-to-end. Speculative decoding helps on code, hurts on English, and agent sessions are prefill-bound.
summary: Kai walks through the headline that Qwen 3.8 27B hit 200 tokens/s on an M5 Max using the Lithos Metal engine. He first derives the memory-bandwidth ceiling (about 38 tok/s for the 40-core M5 Max at 4-bit) and explains that speculative decoding with a 1.1 GB drafter is how the engine goes past it. The 168/127 tok/s figures in the README are compute projections that assume 6 accepted tokens per 8-token pass and exclude drafting and rewind, and the chart comparing against MLX and Ollama times different scopes. The one end-to-end run in the repo (four prompts, 128 tokens) averaged 2.5 accepted guesses per round and about 80 tok/s, and acceptance depends heavily on text type: code is about 1.5x faster than OMLX, while English is about 10% slower, and a bad drafter can make English slower than no drafting at all. For agent workloads the video argues prefill dominates (about 6 input tokens per output token, with prefill about 2.5x slower than OMLX at the time), so a full session takes roughly 18 minutes on Lithos versus 13 on OMLX until fixes ship. Hardware support is limited to the 40-core M5 Max with measured kernels, the engine handles one generation at a time (429 for concurrent requests), and there is a correctness report of drafted output diverging from plain output at temperature 0 on an experimental backend. The closing advice is to ask what was counted, what was written, and to time whole tasks in minutes.

key_ideas.idea: Decode is memory-bandwidth bound, so the tok/s ceiling is roughly bandwidth divided by bytes read per token.
key_ideas.detail: A 27B model at 4-bit is about 16 GB read per token; the 40-core M5 Max at about 614 GB/s gives a ceiling of about 38 tok/s. A plain-decode run in August hit 30.5 tok/s, about 80% of that ceiling. The 32-core M5 Max is 460 GB/s and the base M5 is 153 GB/s.

key_ideas.idea: Speculative decoding lets the big model verify several drafted tokens per memory read.
key_ideas.detail: A 1.1 GB drafter (dSpark) proposes 7 tokens, and the 27B model checks all of them in one pass plus one guaranteed token. If all are accepted, that is 8 tokens per read. If the first is wrong, you get 1 token and still paid for drafting. The technique came from a DeepSeek paper in July, which reported 60-85% faster per-user output on DeepSeek's servers.

key_ideas.idea: The 168 and 200 tok/s headlines are projections, not measured generation rates.
key_ideas.detail: The README's 168 tok/s (128-token context) and 127 tok/s (32k context) are compute projections assuming 6 accepted tokens per 8-token pass, with drafting, acceptance checks and rewind left out. The README itself says they are not end-to-end rates. The 200 headline drops the context length and acceptance rate.

key_ideas.idea: The one measured end-to-end run in the repo gave about 80 tok/s, and the gap to 200 is the acceptance rate.
key_ideas.detail: Across about 150 draft-check-commit rounds on four prompts (code, math, chat, plain text) at 128 tokens, the drafter averaged 2.5 accepted guesses per round, roughly one in three, for about 80 tok/s. Six accepted guesses would be needed to reach the projected number.

key_ideas.idea: Speculative decoding speed depends on how predictable the text is. Code wins, English can lose.
key_ideas.detail: Code repeats (brackets, imports, variable names), so a code-trained drafter guesses well. Prose is less predictable. On the same M5 Max, Lithos beat OMLX on code (59 vs 55 tok/s, and 49 vs 39 at 32k context) but was slower on English (34 vs 38). An untuned fallback on an M4 Pro dropped English to 2 tok/s with drafting on versus 7 with it off.

key_ideas.idea: Agent sessions are prefill-bound, so prefill speed matters more than the headline decode number.
key_ideas.detail: In an AgentPerfLocal replay of 8 tasks over 168 turns on Qwen 3.8 27B, about 196k new input tokens and 31k output tokens were processed even after caching, a 6:1 ratio. Lithos prefill was 374 tok/s versus OMLX's 948 on a 4k prompt. Per session, Lithos took about 18 minutes against OMLX's 13. The video estimates about 10 minutes at 80 tok/s, and about 6 at 200, once the merged prefill fixes ship.

key_ideas.idea: Support and safety are narrow: only one chip has measured kernels, requests run one at a time, and drafted output can diverge.
key_ideas.detail: Only the 40-core M5 Max has tuned kernels. The 32-core M5 Max, M4 Max and M5 Pro use an unmeasured fallback with no mega-kernel fusion. There is no M6 backend, and the M6 Mac Mini's ceiling is about 10 tok/s. The engine serves one generation at a time (a second request gets a 429). An October 14 report shows drafted output drifting from plain output at temperature 0 on an experimental backend, which breaks the expected identical-output property.

key_ideas.idea: Three questions for any speed headline: what was counted, what was written, and how long a whole task takes.
key_ideas.detail: Counted: peak, average, a sum across concurrent users, or a projection assuming perfect guesses. Written: code, English, math, or copying from the prompt (a 381 tok/s RTX 3090 result came from copying a 25k-token document back out). Time: wall-clock minutes from enter to done, because that captures reading, drafting and misses together.

techniques.name: Estimate decode ceiling from memory bandwidth
techniques.how: Divide memory bandwidth (GB/s) by the bytes of weights read per token (about 16 GB for a 27B model at 4-bit). Example: 614 / 16 is about 38 tok/s on the 40-core M5 Max. Measured plain decode reached about 80% of this (30.5 tok/s).
techniques.when: Sanity-checking any local-LLM speed claim before reading the benchmark. A number far above the ceiling implies speculation, batching, or a different scope.

techniques.name: Speculative decoding with a small drafter
techniques.how: A small drafter (dSpark, 1.1 GB) proposes 7 tokens. The big model verifies all 7 plus one guaranteed token in one weight-reading pass, accepting tokens up to the first mismatch. Output should match plain decoding.
techniques.when: Decode is bandwidth-bound and the text is predictable, such as code or copying from the prompt. Avoid or benchmark first on prose, where acceptance can be low enough to be slower than baseline.

techniques.name: Measure acceptance rate alongside tok/s
techniques.how: Track accepted guesses per round (the video's run averaged 2.5 of 7). Report it with the throughput number, and split results by prompt type (code, math, chat, plain text).
techniques.when: Evaluating any speculative-decoding setup. Without acceptance rate, the throughput number can't be interpreted.

techniques.name: Estimate whole-session time from prefill and decode rates
techniques.how: Session time is approximately input_tokens / prefill_rate + output_tokens / decode_rate. The video's example: 31k output at 55 tok/s is about 9.5 min, plus 196k input at about 900 tok/s is under 4 min, for about 13 min total.
techniques.when: Comparing engines for agent workloads, where input tokens dominate. Use the calculation to decide which engine to deploy, instead of trusting headline decode speed.

techniques.name: Time the whole task instead of quoting tok/s
techniques.how: Run the same real prompt or agent task on the current and candidate engine, with the same script and settings, at least three runs each. Record minutes from enter to done.
techniques.when: Any local-model switch decision. This captures prefill, drafting, and rejected guesses, which tok/s hides.

techniques.name: Lower thinking-mode effort for local Qwen
techniques.how: The speaker says to reduce Qwen's thinking effort from x-high, because one M5 Max owner measured x-high at about 5.5x the tokens of thinking-off mode. No specific flag or config key is shown.
techniques.when: Running a thinking-capable local model where wall-clock time matters more than maximum reasoning.

techniques.name: Read the benchmark repo before the blog post
techniques.how: Check the README's own caveats, the measurement study in the repo, and the open GitHub issues before relying on the headline. The speaker found the honest numbers were in the README and the study.
techniques.when: Evaluating any early-stage inference engine whose headline and docs disagree.

tools: Apple M5 Max / M5 Pro / M4 Max / M4 Pro / M6 Mac Mini (hardware)

numbers.claim: Ceiling: about 16 GB read per token and 614 GB/s on the 40-core M5 Max gives about 38 tok/s
Plain 4-bit decode on M5 Max (August) measured 30.5 tok/s, about 80% of ceiling
Bandwidth: 32-core M5 Max 460 GB/s, base M5 153 GB/s, M6 Mac Mini assumed 170 GB/s (about 10 tok/s ceiling)
Drafter guesses 7 tokens; big model verifies in one pass of 8 rows; drafter is 1.1 GB
DeepSeek reported 60-85% faster per-user output with speculative decoding
README projections: 168 tok/s at 128-token context, 127 tok/s at 32k; target verify pass about 36 ms; assumes 6 accepted tokens per 8-token pass
Measured end-to-end run (Oct 3 study, four prompts, 128 tokens, about 150 rounds): 2.5 accepted guesses per round (about 1 in 3), about 80 tok/s
Headline timeline: 30.5 tok/s (mid-Aug), D-Flash 2 at 70 (~4 days later), Splash at 144 (Sep 19), Lithos at 200 (Oct 8)
M5 Pro user on Splash: 50-60 tok/s on code; MLTF 200+ was four summed concurrent requests, single user about 70
RTX 3090 hit 381 tok/s copying a 25k-token document (15 of 16 guesses correct), vs about 133 tok/s on ordinary chat
Lithos vs OMLX (M5 Max 40-core, 128 GB, same script, three runs): code 59 vs 55 tok/s; at 32k context 49 vs 39 (25% lead); English 34 vs 38 tok/s
MLX D-SPARK on M4 Pro: about 3x on math, 2.4x on code, under 2x on chat
Untuned fallback on M4 Pro: English 2 tok/s with drafting on vs 7 with it off
AgentPerfLocal: 8 tasks, 168 turns; about 196k new input tokens and 31k output tokens after caching (6:1)
Prefill: Lithos 374 tok/s vs OMLX 948 tok/s on a 4k prompt; 16k prompt took 43 s on Lithos vs 17 s on OMLX
Estimated session time: OMLX about 13 min (9.5 min writing + under 4 min reading); Lithos as shipped about 18 min; about 10 min at 80 tok/s and about 6 min at 200 tok/s after prefill fixes
Repo is 11 days old with 35 open issues and PRs at time of the video
x-high thinking mode produced about 5.5x the tokens of thinking-off mode (one owner's measurement)

hot_takes: The '200 tok/s' headline is a projection with optimistic acceptance, not a measured rate; the measured end-to-end figure in the repo is about 80 tok/s.
Headlines in this space have roughly doubled every few weeks (30.5, 70, 144, 200), and each one counts something different (peak, sum, copy, projection).
For agent workloads, prefill speed matters more than headline decode speed; Lithos's 200 headline would finish a session in about 6 minutes only after prefill is fixed.
Speculative decoding can make English output slower than no drafting at all, so turning on the 'fast mode' is not always a win.
Qwen thinking at x-high can produce about 5.5x the tokens of thinking-off mode, so reducing reasoning effort may be a bigger speed lever than the engine.

relevance.why: InferCraft (L2B) runs speculative decoding and KV-cache strategies on one RTX 5090. The video's acceptance-rate dependence, prefill-vs-decode split, and single-request 429 behavior apply directly to how InferCraft should be benchmarked.
relevance.action: Add acceptance rate (accepted tokens per round) and per-prompt-type breakdown to InferCraft's speculative-decoding benchmarks, and add an AgentPerfLocal-style replayed agent-session benchmark that reports prefill and decode separately plus wall-clock time to finish the session.

relevance.why: No direct bearing on the Claude Code harness; the video is about local-model engines.
